Diesel prices in NI at highest level since Iran war began
Image source, EPA
By John Campbell
Economics and business editor, BBC News NI
Published
2 October 2026, 09:46 BST
Updated 4 hours ago
Diesel prices in Northern Ireland are at their highest level since the Iran conflict began, according to Consumer Council data.
It shows that over the past week the average price of a litre of diesel was 193.3p.
That is below the record average of 197.2p in the summer of 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, however some filling stations have already being charging £2 a litre.
Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, a litre of diesel cost about 132p.
The Consumer Council data also suggests average petrol prices in Northern Ireland reached a post-Iran war high of 167.2p a litre over the past week.
That compares with about 124p a litre before the conflict began but well below the peak of almost 190p in the summer of 2022.
Data from the UK's Department for Transport shows that motorists in Northern Ireland are more reliant on diesel than those in other parts of the UK.
The figures suggest that just over half the private cars on Northern Ireland's roads use diesel, compared with a UK average of a third.
Sales of new diesel cars in Northern Ireland have fallen sharply in recent years in line with a trend across the UK.
Trump threatens diesel export ban
Diesel prices in the UK hit a record high this week and are hovering at just under 200p a litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.
The conflict in the Middle East has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region - that has caused the price of fuels made from oil to surge.
US President Donald Trump has said he may call on European countries to release some of their diesel reserves .
He is also considering a ban on US exports of the fuel as American drivers also face higher fuel costs.
Such a move could bring prices down significantly in the US.
But experts warn that it would put further pressure on diesel prices in other countries, unless they can access further supplies.
The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels a day.
While UK refineries produce more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel to meet the country's needs.
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of the imports coming from the US.
What do drivers think?
Image caption, Niall Greenan said he relies on his diesel car for work and the school run
At a forecourt in Belfast, Niall Greenan said higher diesel prices had not changed how much he drives, but he said he felt for those whose livelihoods depended on being on the road.
"I've got a lot of friends who are taxi drivers and work in transport and I just have to feel for them because it's just eaten up a lot of the profit margin," he said.
"I can see why it would put people off driving and put them onto foot or public transport for sure."
Greenan still needs his own car for work and the school run, meaning the extra cost is something he has to absorb.
Image caption, Darcy Defty said she was choosing to walk more as fuel prices rise
Student Darcy Defty says higher fuel prices had already changed how much she drives.
"Your money just wouldn't go as far. You'd put £20 in and it just wouldn't get you the same distance.
"Now it's just on top of insurance and then paying for the car as well. It's just not affordable."
She said she now prefers to walk where possible rather than pay for fuel.
Image caption, Gary Robins commutes from Bangor to Belfast for work
Gary Robins, who commutes from Bangor to Belfast for work, said rising diesel prices were adding significantly to his weekly costs.
"I used to fill my work van up once a week. It's now creeping in where it's near enough twice a week."
He said the higher prices were having a particular impact on working people who rely on their vehicles to get to work.
"Probably once you start going up to £2.50, £3 a litre, that's when it's going to start really biting into the pocket."
Image caption, Sara McBarron says she searches for cheaper places to fill up
Sara McBarron said she was increasingly looking for the cheapest places to fill up and would travel around 20 minutes for lower fuel prices.
She is also walking and using public transport more, but said higher bus fares mean that can be costly too.
"Both of them are just as bad as each other honestly."
